Headroom · design feedback · Aug 2026

Two things Ridd would try

His voice notes reduce to two ideas: the green bars out-shout the numbers they support, and the provider header rows restate what the account list already shows. Below — the current build, then mockups of each interpretation, built with Headroom's real dark-scheme tokens.

Note 1 · the bars

"Do they actually have to be green bars? They ask for so much attention they almost overpower things — but the only point of the bar is to back up the 80% and the 74%. It's a secondary visual. Play with a gradient — really subtle on the left, approaching green toward the end. Or make it more like a knob or a line. I think you could make this beautiful and more minimal if you thought about how to remove the green bars."

Note 2 · the hierarchy

"The Claude and Codex logos take up their own row, and then '2 accounts' — of course I know, I can see the two accounts. What if you just used the icon, not the full word, to the left of Personal and Work? Then do you even need the separation between Claude and Codex — what if it's one card with dividing lines? Honestly what I'd try: a really small header with a faint divider, then the personal section, another divider, then work. I almost never add dividing lines, but here they'd help you parse it."

Condensed from iMessage auto-transcription — wording cleaned, meaning preserved.

Theme 1 · Round 2

Quieter, stranger

Eight more ways to demote the bar. The framing rule (via Emil Kowalski): this popover gets opened dozens of times a day, and surfaces seen that often should default to calm — color is an event, not a state. A few of these lean into James McDonald territory: dimensional and tactile but restrained, where light and depth do the work color used to do.

Hue travel
Neutral gray resolving into color at the reading edge
His literal words

Weekly· Resets in 3d 23h38%left
Weekly (Fable)· Resets in 3d 23h12%left

A was an opacity fade; this is a saturation fade — "really subtle in color, approaching green toward the end." The fill stays fully opaque (so the length still reads at a squint) but only earns its hue near the value. Slightly more legible than A on the glass card because the tail never drops below the track's luminance.

I
Ghost fill, bright cap
The region whispers; a 3.5pt cap at the edge speaks

5-hour· Resets in 3h 11m72%left
Weekly· Resets in 3d 23h38%left
Weekly (Fable)· Resets in 3d 23h12%left

Full-saturation ink shrinks from the whole region to ~3pt — the cap is exactly where your eye needs to land to read the value, so the signal survives intact. Unlike the gradients, severity color stays equally visible at 5% and 95%. The ghost region keeps the squint-read.

Console ticks — quiet tint, full color only on the last lit segment

5-hour· Resets in 3h 11m72%left

Quarter ticks make it an instrument, not a progress bar. This is the ring-shadow/light-glow elevation language you already use, applied to the meter itself.

Included because it reframes the question.

Close cousin of the compact widget-tier meters.

Round 3

The instrument, explored

K wins, so this round works inside it: the E and F layouts rebuilt on recessed bars, then four takes on how much color the instrument actually needs. The organizing idea is a loudness budget — every element gets ink proportional to how much it matters right now: critical > low > numerals > structure > healthy fills. Scannability comes from the ranking being strict, not from any single treatment.

Where this lands

Build 1 and 2 first — same layout, one fill variable — and flip between them in --demo mode on the real glass card. That settles the only genuinely open design question (does healthy get a hue?) with evidence instead of debate. Keep 4 in your pocket if you want something shipped this week, and fall back to 3 if the flat list turns out to fight the provider-state architecture.

  • The flat list (1/2) needs an answer for provider-scoped states — capability failures, Connect/Waiting cards, per-account sign-in rows — before it’s more than a picture. 3 and 4 inherit today’s answers for free.
  • Everything here is tuned dark-first. The frosted fills, blooms, and recessed wells all need a light-mode pass, and the same live glass-card check that killed the H3a bands (G1 review).
  • The severity ramp is load-bearing (UI-01): whichever fill recipe wins, keep green→amber→red semantics intact and propagate the recipe to the widget meters through the shared tokens — that keeps popover and widgets one family.
  • Label: L2 (true small caps, wide) is the best fit for the instrument language — engraved register, no added chrome; L6 (merged identity line) is the density play and stacks with it. L5 (brand-tinted) only makes sense with the graduated fills, never the strict-quiet ones. If the quiet family feels too austere after living with it, W (hue travel in the well) is the first dial to turn, then V.
  • Dividers won their argument (Ridd was right): in the machined language the hairlines read as part of the instrument, not added chrome — but re-run the proximity-vs-chrome comparison once on the live surface.
Built from Ridd's voice notes (Aug 3) · mockups use Headroom's real dark-scheme tokens from BrandColorValues.swift · reference renders via --render-popover (demo fixtures, not live account data)
